_comment: The floor scripts/coverage-gate.sh holds each language to. A pull request
may not drop below these numbers (less a small tolerance for run-to-run
wobble); it is free to leave them exactly where they are.
Raising a number is a deliberate, reviewable commit - which is the point.
Coverage that ratchets automatically records whatever the last green run
happened to hit, including a run that got lucky; coverage that ratchets by
hand records a decision that the new floor is one the project intends to
keep standing on.
test code, and measuring how thoroughly the tests test themselves is a
number with no meaning.
Raised 24.5 -> 34 when epoch 01 closed. It had sat at 24.5 while the
measured figure was 34.1, which is ten points of slack: a third of the
coverage could have disappeared without the gate saying anything. A floor
that far below the floor you are standing on is not a ratchet, it is a
number. Set at 34 rather than 34.1 so ordinary run-to-run wobble does not
fail a change that added nothing.
One floor per Go module, because a single number over one module was what
this was: scripts/contractor alone had a floor, and the other six modules -
two of which no task even ran - had none. A combined number also cannot say
which module lost its tests.
The modules are discovered by taskfile.yml rather than listed, and the gate
refuses a key it has no baseline for. So a new module fails until its floor
is written here, which is the decision this file exists to record.
Each is set a little under the figure measured on 2026-09-07, for the same
run-to-run wobble reason the old single number was.
js: measured by vitest over any application code. There is none yet, so
the floor is 0 until there is.
TIER FLOORS are a different measurement and exist for a different reason.
A percentage answers how much of a Go program the tests executed, which is
fair for a unit test and meaningless for a tier whose job is to drive real
infrastructure - an integration test that provisions a cluster and asserts
five things about it covers almost no statements and is worth more than a
hundred that do. So the higher tiers get a count and a floor instead.
The floors may be lowered, deliberately and in the same commit, the way a
coverage floor may: consolidating five test functions into one table is an
improvement and will drop a count. What they refuse is the count dropping
and nobody noticing, which is how a tier that is hard to write quietly
stops being written.
